entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9631"/><div sID="gen16968" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9631"/>6. Jr 3:6-6:30, is a new discourse, delivered in Josiah's reign. It consists of two parts, the former extending to <reference osisRef="Jer.4.3">Jr 4:3</reference>, in which he warns Judah from the example of Israel's doom, and yet promises Israel final restoration; the latter a threat of Babylonian invasion; as Nabopolassar founded the Babylonian empire, 625 B.C., the seventeenth of Josiah, this prophecy is perhaps not earlier than that date (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.5">Jr 4:5</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.14">Jr 5:14</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.1">Jr 6:1</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.1-Jer.22.30">Jr 22:1-30</reference>); and probably not later than the second thorough reformation in the eighteenth year of the same reign.<div eID="gen16968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16969" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">backsliding--</hi>literally, "apostasy"; not merely apostate, but apostasy itself, the essence of it (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.14">Jr 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.22">22</reference>). <div eID="gen16969" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 6. Jr 3:6-6:30, is a new discourse, delivered in Josiah's reign. I said--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.13">2Ki 17:13</reference>).<div eID="gen16970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16971" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sister--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.46">Eze 16:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.2">23:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.4">4</reference>). <div eID="gen16971" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9633"/><div sID="gen16972" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9633"/>8. I saw that, though (whereas) it was for this very reason (namely), because backsliding (apostate) Israel had committed adultery I had put her away (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Ki 17:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.18">18</reference>), and given her a bill of divorce, yet Judah, &c. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.11">Eze 23:11</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen16972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16973" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bill of divorce--</hi>literally, "a writing of cuttings off." The plural implies the completeness of the severance. The use of this metaphor here, as in the former discourse (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.1">Jr 3:1</reference>), implies a close connection between the discourses. The epithets are characteristic; Israel "apostate" (as the Hebrew for "backsliding" is better rendered); Judah, not as yet utterly apostate, but treacherous or faithless.<div eID="gen16973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16974" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also--</hi>herself also, like Israel. <div eID="gen16974" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9634"/><div sID="gen16975" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9634"/><hi type="bold">9. it--</hi>Some take this verse of Judah, to whom the end of <reference osisRef="Jer.3.8">Jr 3:8</reference> refers. But <reference osisRef="Jer.3.10">Jr 3:10</reference> puts Judah in contrast to Israel in this verse. "Yet for all this," referring to the sad example of Israel; if <reference osisRef="Jer.3.9">Jr 3:9</reference> referred to Judah, "she" would have been written in <reference osisRef="Jer.3.10">Jr 3:10</reference>, not "Judah." Translate, "It (the putting away of Israel) had come to pass through ... whoredom; and (that is, for) she (Israel) had defiled the land" &c. [Maurer]. English Version, however, may be explained to refer to Israel.<div eID="gen16975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lightness--</hi>"infamy." [Ewald]. Maurer not so well takes it from the Hebrew root, "voice," "fame." <div eID="gen16976" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9641"/><div sID="gen16991" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9641"/><hi type="bold">16. they shall say no more--</hi>The Jews shall no longer glory in the possession of the ark; it shall not be missed, so great shall be the blessings of the new dispensation. The throne of the Lord, present Himself, shall eclipse and put out of mind the ark of the covenant and the mercy seat between the cherubim, God's former throne. Israel ... together--</hi>Two distinct apostasies, that of Israel and that of Judah, were foretold (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.8">Jr 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.10">10</reference>). The two have never been united since the Babylonish captivity; therefore their joint restoration must be still future (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">Is 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.16-Ezek.37.22">Eze 37:16-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.1.11">Ho 1:11</reference>).<div eID="gen16997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16998" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">north--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.3.12">Jr 3:12</reference>).<div eID="gen16998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">land ... given ... inheritance--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Amos.9.15">Am 9:15</reference>). <div eID="gen16999" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9644"/><div sID="gen17000" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9644"/>19. The good land covenanted to Abraham is to be restored to his seed. But the question arises, How shall this be done?<div eID="gen17000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put ... among ... children--</hi>the Greek for adoption means, literally, "putting among the sons."<div eID="gen17001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17002" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the children--</hi>that is, My children. "How shall I receive thee back into My family, after thou hast so long forsaken Me for idols?" The answer is, they would acknowledge Him as "Father," and no longer turn away from Him. God assumes the language of one wondering how so desperate apostates could be restored to His family and its privileges (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.3">Eze 37:3</reference>; Calvin makes it, How the race of Abraham can be propagated again, being as it were dead); yet as His purpose has decreed it so, He shows how it shall be effected, namely, they shall receive from Him the spirit of adoption to cry, "My Father" (<reference osisRef="John.1.12">Joh 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Ga 4:6</reference>). The elect are "children" already in God's purpose; this is the ground of the subsequent realization of this relationship (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.5">Ep 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.13">He 2:13</reference>).<div eID="gen17002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17003" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pleasant land--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.11.5">Jr 11:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.6">Eze 20:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.16">Da 11:16</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen17003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17004" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heritage of ... hosts--</hi>a heritage the most goodly of all nations [Maurer]; or a "heritage possessed by powerful hosts" (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.38">De 4:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.2.9">Am 2:9</reference>). The rendering "splendors," instead of "hosts," is opposed by the fact that the Hebrew for "splendor" is not found in the plural. <div eID="gen17004" type="x-p"/>
